Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a traffic stop becomes unlawful when officers extend it beyond the time reasonably needed without reasonable suspicion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Tenth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. The officers unlawfully prolonged the traffic stop beyond the time reasonably needed to complete its mission, and they had no reasonable suspicion to justify the extension.

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment. The court analyzes it under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 20 (1968). *United States v. Mendez*, 118 F.3d 1426, 1429 (10th Cir. 1997). The analysis has two parts. The first asks whether the stop was justified at its inception. The second asks whether the officer's actions were reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified the stop. *Id.*; *United States v. Karam*, 496 F.3d 1157, 1161–62 (10th Cir. 2007). This appeal concerns the second part.

**A. The authority for a traffic stop ends when its mission is, or reasonably should have been, completed.**

A stop's tolerable duration is set by its mission, which is addressing the traffic violation that justified it. *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 354–57 (2015). Authority for the seizure "ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are—or reasonably should have been—completed." *Id.* at 354. A stop that is lawful at its start "can become unlawful if it is prolonged beyond the time reasonably required." *Illinois v. Caballes*, 543 U.S. 405, 407 (2005).

The Tenth Circuit has applied this principle for decades. An officer may request a driver's license and registration, run background checks, and issue a citation or warning. *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000); *Karam*, 496 F.3d at 1161–62. Once those tasks are done, the officer must ordinarily let the driver go. The officer may continue the detention only if the driver consents or the officer has an objectively reasonable and articulable suspicion of illegal activity. *West*, 219 F.3d at 1176; *United States v. Gonzalez-Lerma*, 14 F.3d 1479, 1483 (10th Cir. 1994). *See also United States v. Salzano*, 158 F.3d 1107, 1111 (10th Cir. 1998). Unrelated inquiries and investigative detours that add time to the stop do not fit within the stop's mission. Without reasonable suspicion, they make the continued seizure unreasonable. *Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 355–57.

**B. The officers prolonged the stop after its mission was complete.**

[Insert record facts: time the stop began, time the license and registration checks were completed, the point at which the officers had everything needed to issue a citation or warning, and the length and purpose of the added detention, such as questioning, a request for consent, or waiting for a canine unit. Cite the record.] By that point the officers had done everything the traffic violation required. Any further detention was a new seizure. It was lawful only if supported by independent reasonable suspicion or a valid consent. The record shows no valid consent. [Confirm.] The question is therefore whether the officers had reasonable suspicion.

**C. The officers lacked reasonable suspicion to justify the extended detention.**

Reasonable suspicion requires a particularized and objective basis for suspecting the specific person detained of criminal activity. It is not satisfied by an inchoate hunch. *Terry*, 392 U.S. at 21–22; *Karam*, 496 F.3d at 1162. The Tenth Circuit has repeatedly refused to find reasonable suspicion based on factors that are consistent with innocent travel. *United States v. Santos*, 403 F.3d 1120, 1125–26 (10th Cir. 2005), is an example. The court there examined the facts the officer cited, including the driver's nervousness and aspects of the travel itinerary. It held that they did not, singly or together, justify prolonging the detention. *Id.* at 1125–33. *See also Gonzalez-Lerma*, 14 F.3d at 1484–86 (holding that the facts known to the officer did not support detention beyond the traffic stop's purpose).

The same result follows here. The factors the Government relies on [list: e.g., nervousness, travel plans, rental vehicle, air freshener, etc.] are the kind of generic, innocent-travel facts that this Court has found insufficient. Many law-abiding motorists display them during a roadside encounter with police. Officers cannot assemble reasonable suspicion from such facts after the fact, or after the stop has already been extended. The detention must be justified by what the officers knew when the mission of the stop ended. *See Rodriguez*, 575 U.S. at 357. At that point the officers had only a hunch.

**D. The remedy is suppression.**

Because the officers extended the stop without reasonable suspicion or consent, the continued seizure violated the Fourth Amendment. The evidence obtained during and as a result of that unlawful detention was fruit of the illegality. The district court should have suppressed it. This Court should reverse the denial of the motion to suppress and vacate the conviction.
